{{Short description|Class of games in game theory}}
'''Congestion games''' (CG) are a class of games in [[game theory]]. They represent situations which commonly occur in roads, [[communication networks]], [[oligopoly]] markets and [[Habitat|natural habitats]]. There is a set of resources (e.g. roads or communication links); there are several players who need resources (e.g. drivers or network users); each player chooses a subset of these resources (e.g. a path in the network); the delay in each resource is determined by the number of players choosing a subset that contains this resource. The cost of each player is the sum of delays among all resources he chooses. Naturally, each player wants to minimize his own delay; however, each player's choices impose a negative [[externality]] on the other players, which may lead to inefficient outcomes.

The research of congestion games was initiated by the American economist [[Robert W. Rosenthal]] in 1973.<ref name=":1">{{citation |last=Rosenthal |first=Robert W. |title=A class of games possessing pure-strategy Nash equilibria |journal=International Journal of Game Theory |volume=2 |pages=65–67 |year=1973 |doi=10.1007/BF01737559 |mr=0319584|s2cid=121904640 }}.</ref> He proved that every congestion game has a Nash equilibrium in [[pure strategies]] (aka ''pure Nash equilibrium'', PNE). During the proof, he in fact proved that every congestion game is an [[potential game|exact potential game]]. Later, Monderer and Shapley<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Monderer |first1=Dov |last2=Shapley |first2=Lloyd S. |date=1996-05-01 |title=Potential Games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825696900445 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=124–143 |doi=10.1006/game.1996.0044 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> proved a converse result: any game with an exact potential function is equivalent to some congestion game. Later research focused on questions such as:

* Does the existence of equilibrium, as well as the existence of a potential function, extend to more general models of congestion games?
* What is the quantitative [[Price of anarchy in congestion games|inefficiency of congestion games]]?
* What is the [[Computational complexity of mathematical operations|computational complexity]] of finding an equilibrium?

== Example ==
[[File:Congestion-diagram.svg|thumb|right|300px|The directed graph for a simple congestion game.]]
Consider a traffic net where two players originate at point {{mvar|O}} and need to get to point {{mvar|T}}. Suppose that node {{mvar|O}} is connected to node {{mvar|T}} via two paths: {{math|{{var|O}}-{{var|A}}-{{var|T}}}} and {{math|{{var|O}}-{{var|B}}-{{var|T}}}}, where {{mvar|A}} is a little closer than {{mvar|B}} (i.e. {{mvar|A}} is more likely to be chosen by each player), as in the picture at the right.

The roads from both connection points to {{mvar|T}} get easily congested, meaning the more players pass through a point, the greater the delay of each player becomes, so having both players go through the same connection point causes extra delay. Formally, the delay in each of {{math|{{var|A}}{{var|T}}}} and {{math|{{var|B}}{{var|T}}}} when {{mvar|x}} players go there is <math>x^2</math>.

A good outcome in this game will be for the two players to "coordinate" and pass through different connection points. Can such an outcome be achieved?

The following matrix expresses the costs of the players in terms of delays depending on their choices:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; width:150px; height:150px" border="1" 
|+Cost Matrix
|- 
! {{diagonal split header|p1|p2}} !! OAT !! OBT
|- 
! OAT 
| (5,5) || (2,3) 
|- 
! OBT 
| (3,2) || (6,6) 
|}
The pure [[Nash equilibria]] in this game are (OAT,OBT) and (OBT,OAT): any unilateral change by one of the players increases the cost of this player (note that the values in the table are costs, so players prefer them to be smaller). In this example, the Nash equilibrium is ''efficient'' - the players choose different lanes and the sum of costs is minimal.

In contrast, suppose the delay in each of {{mvar|A}}{{mvar|T}} and {{mvar|B}}{{mvar|T}} when {{mvar|x}} players go there is <math>0.8 x</math>. Then the cost matrix is:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center; width:150px; height:150px" border="1" 
|+Cost Matrix
|- 
! {{diagonal split header|p1|p2}} !! OAT !! OBT
|- 
! OAT 
| (2.6,2.6) || (1.8,2.8) 
|- 
! OBT 
| (2.8,1.8) || (3.6,3.6) 
|}
Now, the only pure Nash equilibrium is {{tmath|(OAT,OAT)}}: any player switching to OBT increases his cost from 2.6 to 2.8. An equilibrium still exists, but it is not efficient: the sum of costs is 5.2, while the sum of cost in {{tmath|(OAT,OBT)}} and {{tmath|(OBT,OAT)}} is 4.6.

==Basic result==

=== Notation ===
The basic definition of a CG has the following components.
* A base set {{mvar|E}} of congestible elements (also called ''resources'' or ''factors''). In the above example, {{mvar|E}} is the set of roads ({{mvar|O}}{{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|A}}{{mvar|T}}, {{mvar|O}}{{mvar|B}} and {{mvar|B}}{{mvar|T}}).
* A set of {{mvar|n}} players. In the above example <math>n=2</math>.
* A [[finite set]] of strategies <math>S_i</math> for each player, where each strategy <math>P \in S_i</math> is a subset of {{mvar|E}}. 
** In the above example, both players have the same set of strategies: <math>S_1 = S_2 = \{ \{OA,AT\}, \{OB,BT\} \}</math>. CGs in which all players have the same set of strategies are called '''symmetric CGs'''. In general, different players may have different sets, for example, if each player has a different source and/or a different target. Such CGs are called '''asymmetric''' '''CGs'''.
** In general, a strategy can be any subset of {{mvar|E}}. CGs in which a strategy can only be a path in a given graph (as in the above example) are called '''network CGs'''. CGs in which a strategy can only be a single resource are called '''singleton CGs'''.
* For each element <math>e\in E</math> and a vector of strategies <math>(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n)</math>, the ''load'' is defined as <math>x_e = \#\{ i : e \in P_i \}</math>.
* For each element <math>e\in E</math> there is a '''delay function''' <math>d_e : \mathbb{N} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> (also called '''latency function''' or '''cost function'''). Given a vector of strategies, the delay on {{mvar|e}} is <math>d_e(x_e)</math>. Each <math>d_e</math> is assumed to be positive and [[Monotonic function|monotone increasing]].
* Given a strategy <math>P_i</math>, player {{mvar|i}} experiences delay <math>\textstyle \sum_{e \in P_i} d_e(x_e)</math>; each player wants to minimize his delay.
* A ''Nash equilibrium'' is a vector of strategies <math>(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n)</math> such that, for each player {{mvar|i}}, replacing <math>P_i</math> with a different strategy <math>Q_i</math> would not decrease the delay experienced by {{mvar|i}}.

=== Existence of Nash equilibria ===
Every CG has a [[Nash equilibria|Nash equilibrium]] in [[pure strategies]]. This can be shown by constructing a ''potential function'' that assigns a value to each outcome.<ref name=":1" /> Moreover, this construction will also show that iterated [[best response]] finds a Nash equilibrium. Define <math>\textstyle\Phi = \sum_{e \in E} \sum_{k=1}^{x_e} d_e(k)</math>. Note that this function is ''not'' the social welfare <math>\textstyle\sum_{e \in E} x_e d_e(x_e)</math>, but rather a discrete integral of sorts. The critical property of a potential function for a congestion game is that if one player switches strategy, the change in his delay is equal to the change in the potential function.

Consider the case when player {{mvar|i}} switches from <math>P_i</math> to <math>Q_i</math>. Elements that are in both of the strategies
remain unaffected, elements that the player leaves (i.e. <math>e \in P_i - Q_i</math>) decrease the potential by <math>d_e (x_e)</math>, and the elements the player joins (i.e. <math>e \in Q_i - P_i</math>) increase the potential by <math>d_e(x_e+1)</math>. This change in potential is precisely the change in delay for player {{mvar|i}}, so <math>\Phi</math> is in fact a potential function.

Now observe that any minimum of <math>\Phi</math> is a pure Nash equilibrium. Fixing all but one player, any improvement in strategy by that player corresponds to decreasing <math>\Phi</math>, which cannot happen at a minimum. Now since there are a finite number of configurations and each <math>d_e</math> is monotone, there exists an equilibrium.

The existence of a potential function has an additional implication, called the '''finite improvement property (FIP)'''. If we start with any strategy-vector, pick a player arbitrarily, and let him change his strategy to a better strategy for him, and repeat, then the sequence of improvements must be finite (that is, the sequence will not cycle). This is because each such improvement strictly increases the potential.

=== Extensions ===
Below we present various extensions and variations on the basic CG model.

==<span class="anchor" id="nonatomic"></span>Nonatomic congestion games==
A '''nonatomic''' '''CG''' is the limit of a standard CG with ''n'' players, as <math>n \rightarrow \infty</math>. As in any [[nonatomic game]], there is a continuum of players, the players are considered "infinitesimally small", and each individual player has a negligible effect on the congestion. Nonatomic CGs were studied by Milchtaich,<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=1996 |title=Congestion Models of Competition |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2463089 |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=147 |issue=5 |pages=760–783 |doi=10.1086/285878 |jstor=2463089 |bibcode=1996ANat..147..760M |s2cid=55004212 |issn=0003-0147}}</ref> Friedman,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Friedman |first=Eric J. |date=1996-09-01 |title=Dynamics and Rationality in Ordered Externality Games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825696900743 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=65–76 |doi=10.1006/game.1996.0074 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Blonsky,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Blonski |first=Matthias |date=1999-08-01 |title=Anonymous Games with Binary Actions |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825698906996 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=171–180 |doi=10.1006/game.1998.0699 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Roughgarden and Tardos.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=Tim |last2=Tardos |first2=Éva |date=2004-05-01 |title=Bounding the inefficiency of equilibria in nonatomic congestion games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089982560300188X |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=389–403 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2003.06.004 |s2cid=10778635 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

* We keep {{mvar|E}} a ''finite'' set of congestible elements.
* Instead of recognizing {{mvar|n}} players, as in the discrete case, we have {{mvar|n}} ''types'' of players, where each type {{mvar|i}} is associated with a number <math>r_i</math>, representing the ''rate'' of traffic for that type.
* Each agent in type ''i'' picks a strategy from the strategy set <math>S_i</math>.
* As before, the delay functions <math>d_e</math> are monotone and positive, but we now add the assumption that they are [[Continuous function|continuous]] as well.
* We allow players in a type to distribute fractionally over their strategy set. That is, for every strategy <math>P \in S_i</math>, let <math>f_P</math> denote the fraction of players in type {{mvar|i}} using strategy {{mvar|P}}. By definition, <math>\textstyle \sum_{P\in S_i} f_P = r_i</math>.
* For each element <math>e\in E</math>, the ''load'' is defined as the sum of fractions of players using ''e'', that is, <math>x_e = \sum_{P\ni e} f_P</math>.

=== Existence of equilibria in nonatomic CGs ===
Strategies are now collections of strategy profiles <math>f_P</math>. For a strategy set <math>S_i</math> of size {{mvar|n}}, the collection of all valid profiles is a [[Compact space|compact subset]] of <math>[0,r_i]^n</math>. We now define the potential function as <math>\textstyle \Phi = \sum_{e\in E} \int_0^{x_e} d_e(z) \, dz</math>, replacing the discrete integral with the standard one.

As a function of the strategy, <math>\Phi</math> is continuous: <math>d_e</math> is continuous by assumption, and <math>x_e</math> is a continuous function of the strategy. Then by the [[extreme value theorem]], <math>\Phi</math> attains its global minimum.

The final step is to show that a minimum of <math>\Phi</math> is indeed a Nash equilibrium. Assume for contradiction that there exists a collection of <math>f_P</math> that minimize <math>\Phi</math> but are not a Nash equilibrium. Then for some type {{mvar|i}}, there exists some improvement <math>Q\in S_i</math> over the current choice {{mvar|P}}. That is, <math>\textstyle
 \sum_{e \in Q} d_e(x_e)
 <
 \sum_{e \in P} d_e(x_e) </math>. The idea now is to take a small amount <math>\delta < f_P</math> of players using strategy {{mvar|P}} and move them to strategy {{mvar|Q}}. Now for any <math>x_e \in Q</math>, we have increased its load by <math>\delta</math>, so its term in <math>\Phi</math> is now <math>\textstyle \int_0^{x_e+\delta} d_e(z)dz</math>. Differentiating the integral, this change is approximately <math>\delta \cdot d_e(x_e)</math>, with error <math>\delta^2</math>. The equivalent analysis of the change holds when we look at edges in {{mvar|P}}.

Therefore, the change in potential is approximately <math>\textstyle \delta (\sum_{e \in Q} d_e(x_e) - \sum_{e \in P} d_e(x_e))</math>, which is less than zero. This is a contradiction, as then <math>\Phi</math> was not minimized. Therefore, a minimum of <math>\Phi</math> must be a Nash equilibrium.

== Splittable congestion games ==
In a '''splittable CG''' (also called '''atomic splittable CG'''), as in an atomic CG, there are finitely many players, each of whom has a certain load to transfer. As in a nonatomic CG, each player can split his load into fractional loads going through different paths, like a transportation company choosing a set of paths for mass transportation. In contrast to a nonatomic CG, each player has a non-negligible effect on the congestion.

Splittable CGs were first analyzed by Ariel Orda, [[Raphael Rom]] and Nachum Shimkin in 1993, in the context of communication networks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Orda |first1=A. |last2=Rom |first2=R. |last3=Shimkin |first3=N. |date=1993-10-01 |title=Competitive routing in multiuser communication networks |journal=IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking |volume=1 |issue=5 |pages=510–521 |doi=10.1109/90.251910 |bibcode=1993ITNet...1..510O |s2cid=1184436 |issn=1558-2566}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=Tim |last2=Schoppmann |first2=Florian |date=2015-03-01 |title=Local smoothness and the price of anarchy in splittable congestion games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022053114000593 |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |series=Computer Science and Economic Theory |language=en |volume=156 |pages=317–342 |doi=10.1016/j.jet.2014.04.005 |issn=0022-0531|url-access=subscription }}</ref> They show that, for a simple network with two nodes and multiple parallel links, the Nash equilibrium is unique under reasonable convexity conditions, and has some interesting monotonicity properties. For general network topologies, more complex conditions are required to guarantee the uniqueness of Nash equilibrium.

In parallel, Haurie and Marcotte<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haurie |first1=A. |last2=Marcotte |first2=P. |date=1985 |title=On the relationship between Nash—Cournot and Wardrop equilibria |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/net.3230150303 |journal=Networks |language=en |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=295–308 |doi=10.1002/net.3230150303 |issn=1097-0037}}</ref> studied splittable CGs in the context of transportation networks. They defined a Nash-Cournot equilibrium and provided conditions for its existence and uniqueness. They showed that, under reasonable conditions, the asymptotic behavior of this NE yield a total flow vector corresponding to a [[Wardrop equilibrium]].

The [[price of anarchy]] in splittable CGs was studied by Gairing, Monien and Tiemann,<ref name=":20" /> Cominetti, Correa and Stier-Moses,<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal |last1=Cominetti |first1=Roberto |last2=Correa |first2=José R. |last3=Stier-Moses |first3=Nicolás E. |date=December 2009 |title=The Impact of Oligopolistic Competition in Networks |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/opre.1080.0653 |journal=Operations Research |volume=57 |issue=6 |pages=1421–1437 |doi=10.1287/opre.1080.0653 |issn=0030-364X}}</ref> Harks,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harks |first=Tobias |date=2011-05-01 |title=Stackelberg Strategies and Collusion in Network Games with Splittable Flow |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00224-010-9269-4 |journal=Theory of Computing Systems |language=en |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=781–802 |doi=10.1007/s00224-010-9269-4 |issn=1433-0490}}</ref> and finally Roughgarden and Schoppmann.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Roughgarden |first1=Tim |last2=Schoppmann |first2=Florian |date=2015-03-01 |title=Local smoothness and the price of anarchy in splittable congestion games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022053114000593 |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |series=Computer Science and Economic Theory |volume=156 |pages=317–342 |doi=10.1016/j.jet.2014.04.005 |issn=0022-0531}}</ref>

Huang<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last=Huang |first=Chien-Chung |date=2013-05-01 |title=Collusion in Atomic Splittable Routing Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00224-012-9421-4 |journal=Theory of Computing Systems |language=en |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=763–801 |doi=10.1007/s00224-012-9421-4 |issn=1433-0490}}</ref> studies the effect of collusion on the [[social cost]] in splittable CGs. He shows that if the network satisfies some natural structural condition, and all delay functions are affine, then collusion decreases the social cost in  equilibrium. But if either of these conditions is not satisfied, collusion might decrease the social cost.

Richman and Shimkin<ref name=":16" /> characterize the networks that guarantee that every splittable CG has a unique PNE. Harks and Timmermans<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Harks |first1=Tobias |last2=Timmermans |first2=Veerle |date=2018-10-01 |title=Uniqueness of equilibria in atomic splittable polymatroid congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10878-017-0166-5 |journal=Journal of Combinatorial Optimization |language=en |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=812–830 |doi=10.1007/s10878-017-0166-5 |issn=1573-2886}}</ref> also study equilibrium uniqueness in atomic splittable polymatroid CGs.

=== Computation ===
Marcotte<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marcotte |first=Patrice |date=1987-11-01 |title=Algorithms for the Network Oligopoly Problem |url=https://doi.org/10.1057/jors.1987.175 |journal=Journal of the Operational Research Society |volume=38 |issue=11 |pages=1051–1065 |doi=10.1057/jors.1987.175 |issn=0160-5682}}</ref> presented four numeric algorithms for computing NE on congested transportation networks, and analyzed their convergence properties. Meunier and Pradeau<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Meunier |first1=Frédéric |last2=Pradeau |first2=Thomas |chapter=A Lemke-Like Algorithm for the Multiclass Network Equilibrium Problem |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2013 |volume=8289 |editor-last=Chen |editor-first=Yiling |editor2-last=Immorlica |editor2-first=Nicole |title=Web and Internet Economics |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-45046-4_30 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=363–376 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-45046-4_30 |isbn=978-3-642-45046-4}}</ref> presented a numeric algorithm, similar to the [[Lemke-Howson algorithm]], for nonatomic network CGs with affine player-specific delay functions. Both these numeric algorithms were not shown to run in polynomial time.

Cominetti, Correa and Stier-Moses<ref name=":17" /> studied splittable CGs with affine player-independent delay functions: <math>d_{e,i}(x) = a_{e}\cdot x_e + b_{e}</math>, where ''x<sub>e</sub>'' is the load on edge ''e'', and ''a<sub>e</sub>'',''b<sub>e</sub>'' are player-independent constants. They showed a convex potential function whose global minima are PNE. This means that epsilon-approximate PNEs can be computed in polytime by [[convex programming]].

Huang<ref name=":18" /> also considered affine player-independent delay functions. He devised a combinatorial algorithm computing an exact PNE for splittable CGs on [[symmetric graph]]s that satisfy a natural structural condition he calls "well-designed" (for example, [[series–parallel graph]]s).

Bhaskar and Lolakapuri<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bhaskar |first1=Umang |last2=Lolakapuri |first2=Phani Raj |date=2018 |editor-last=Azar |editor-first=Yossi |editor2-last=Bast |editor2-first=Hannah |editor3-last=Herman |editor3-first=Grzegorz |title=Equilibrium Computation in Atomic Splittable Routing Games |journal=26th Annual European Symposium on Algorithms (ESA 2018) |series=Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs) |location=Dagstuhl, Germany |publisher=Schloss Dagstuhl – Leibniz-Zentrum für Informatik |volume=112 |pages=58:1–58:14 |doi=10.4230/LIPIcs.ESA.2018.58 |doi-access=free |isbn=978-3-95977-081-1}}</ref> considered splittable network CGs with convex player-independent delay functions. They presented two algorithms for computing approximate PNE: the first is exponential in the number of players, and while the second is exponential in the number of edges. They also show that in general networks, it is NP-hard to decide if there exists a PNE where every player has cost at most some given constant ''C''.

Klimm and Warode<ref>{{Citation |last1=Klimm |first1=Max |title=Complexity and Parametric Computation of Equilibria in Atomic Splittable Congestion Games via Weighted Block Laplacians |date=2020-01-17 |url=http://arxiv.org/abs/1811.08354 |access-date=2025-11-25 |arxiv=1811.08354 |last2=Warode |first2=Philipp}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Klimm |first1=Max |last2=Warode |first2=Philipp |date=2025-10-31 |title=Complexity and Parametric Computation of Equilibria in Atomic Splittable Congestion Games via Weighted Block Laplacians |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/20M1361523 |journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=54 |issue=5 |pages=1241–1293 |doi=10.1137/20M1361523 |issn=0097-5397}}</ref> studied atomic splittable network CGs with affine player-specific delay functions <math>d_{e,i}(x) = a_{e,i}\cdot x_e + b_{e,i}</math>, where ''x<sub>e</sub>'' is the load on edge ''e'', and ''a<sub>ei</sub>'', ''b<sub>ei</sub>'' are player-specific constants. They proved that computing a PNE is [[PPAD-complete]].

Harks and Timmermans<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Harks |first1=Tobias |last2=Timmermans |first2=Veerle |chapter=Equilibrium Computation in Atomic Splittable Singleton Congestion Games |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2017 |volume=10328 |editor-last=Eisenbrand |editor-first=Friedrich |editor2-last=Koenemann |editor2-first=Jochen |title=Integer Programming and Combinatorial Optimization |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-59250-3_36 |language=en |location=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |pages=442–454 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-59250-3_36 |isbn=978-3-319-59250-3}}</ref><ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Harks |first1=Tobias |last2=Timmermans |first2=Veerle |date=2022-07-01 |title=Equilibrium computation in resource allocation games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10107-020-01604-z |journal=Mathematical Programming |language=en |volume=194 |issue=1 |pages=1–34 |doi=10.1007/s10107-020-01604-z |issn=1436-4646}}</ref> study splittable atomic CGs with singleton strategy sets - each player should split his load among the edges (not among the paths). This corresponds to a network of ''m'' parallel edges between the source and the target. They allow player-specific delay functions. The total cost suffered by each player ''i'' is <math>\sum_{e} x_{i,e}\cdot d_{e,i}(x)</math>. They present an algorithm for computing a PNE in time <math>O( (n m)^3 + n^2 m^{14} \log(D/k_0))</math>, where ''n'' is the number of players, ''m'' the number of edges, ''D'' is the maximum player-specific demand, and ''k''<sub>0</sub> the smallest packet size.{{Clarify|date=November 2025}}

They also note that computing a PNE in atomic splittable CGs with singleton strategies and affine delay funcions can be presented as a [[Linear complementarity problem]].<ref name=":19" />

== Weighted congestion games ==
In a '''weighted''' '''CG''', different players may have different effects on the congestion. For example, in a road network, a [[truck]] adds congestion much more than a [[motorcycle]]. Whereas an unweighted CG is an [[anonymous game]], a weighted CG is not anonymous, as the payoff of a player depends not only on the number of players who take each action, but also on their weight.

In general, the weight of a player may depend on the resource ('''resource-specific weights'''): for every player ''i'' and resource ''e'', there is weight <math>w_{i,e}</math>, and the load on the resource ''e'' is <math>x_e = \sum_{i : e \in P_i} w_{i,e}</math>. An important special case is when the weight depends only on the player ('''resource-independent weights'''), that is, each player i has a weight <math>w_i</math>, and <math>x_e = \sum_{i : e \in P_i} w_{i}</math>.

=== Weighted singleton CGs with resource-independent weights ===
Milchtaich<ref name=":2" /> considered the special case of weighted CGs in which each strategy is a single resource ("singleton CG"), the weights are ''resource-independent'', and all players have the same strategy set. The following is proved:

* If all players have the same delay functions, then the game has the finite-improvement property (and thus has a PNE).
* If there are only two strategies (and arbitrarily many players with possibly different delay functions), then the game has the finite-improvement property (and thus has a PNE).
* If there are only two players (with possibly different delay functions), then the game has the finite-best-response property (and thus has a PNE).
* If there are three or more strategies and three or more players with different delay functions, a PNE might not exist.

=== Weighted network CGs ===
Milchtaich considered the special case of weighted CGs in which each strategy is a path in a given [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|undirected graph]] ("network CG"). He proved that every finite game can be represented as a [[weighted network]] congestion game, with nondecreasing (but not necessarily negative) cost-functions.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2013-11-01 |title=Representation of finite games as network congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00182-012-0363-5 |journal=International Journal of Game Theory |language=en |volume=42 |issue=4 |pages=1085–1096 |doi=10.1007/s00182-012-0363-5 |s2cid=253713700 |issn=1432-1270}}</ref> This implies that not every such game has a PNE. Concrete examples of weighted CGs without PNE are given by Libman and Orda,<ref name=":4"/> as well as Goemans Mirrokni and Vetta.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Goemans |first1=M. |last2=Mirrokni |first2=Vahab |last3=Vetta |first3=A. |title=46th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS'05) |chapter=Sink Equilibria and Convergence |date=2005-10-01 |pages=142–151 |doi=10.1109/SFCS.2005.68|isbn=0-7695-2468-0 |s2cid=17850062 }}</ref> This raises the question of what conditions guarantee the existence of PNE.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |chapter=The Equilibrium Existence Problem in Finite Network Congestion Games |date=2006 |editor-last=Spirakis |editor-first=Paul |editor2-last=Mavronicolas |editor2-first=Marios |editor3-last=Kontogiannis |editor3-first=Spyros |title=Internet and Network Economics |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11944874_9 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=4286 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=87–98 |doi=10.1007/11944874_9 |isbn=978-3-540-68141-0}}</ref>

In particular, we say that a certain graph ''G guarantees'' a certain property if every weighted network CG in which the underlying network is ''G'' has that property. Milchtaich<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2015-08-01 |title=Network topology and equilibrium existence in weighted network congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00182-014-0443-9 |journal=International Journal of Game Theory |language=en |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=515–541 |doi=10.1007/s00182-014-0443-9 |s2cid=253723798 |issn=1432-1270|hdl=10419/95995 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> characterized networks that guarantee the existence of PNE, as well as the finite-improvement property, with the additional condition that a player with a lower weight has weakly more allowed strategies (formally, <math>w_i < w_j</math> implies <math>|S_i|\geq |S_j|</math>). He proved that:
* A graph ''G'' guarantees the finite-improvement property iff ''G'' is homeomorphic to either a ''parallel network'' (a graph made of one or more single-edge networks connected [[In Parallel|in parallel]]), or to a parallel network connected [[in series]] with one or two single-edge networks.{{Rp|location=Thm.2}}
* A graph ''G'' guarantees the existence of a PNE iff ''G'' is homeomorphic to a connection [[in series]] of one or more networks from a set of six "allowed networks"; an equivalent condition is that no network from a set of six "forbidden network" is embedded in ''G''.{{Rp|location=Thm.3}}
In the special case in which every player is allowed to use any strategy ("public edges"), there are more networks that guarantee the existence of PNE; a complete characterization of such networks is posed as an [[open problem]].<ref name=":11" />

Milchtaich<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2006-11-01 |title=Network topology and the efficiency of equilibrium |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825605001284 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=321–346 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2005.09.005 |issn=0899-8256|hdl=10419/259308 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> analyzes the effect of [[network topology]] on the ''efficiency'' of PNE:

* A graph ''G'' guarantees that every PNE is Pareto-efficient, iff three simple "forbidden networks" are not embedded in ''G''. 
* A graph ''G'' guarantees that [[Braess's paradox]] does not occur, iff it is a [[Series–parallel graph|series-parallel graph]]. 
Milchtaich<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2005-02-01 |title=Topological Conditions for Uniqueness of Equilibrium in Networks |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/moor.1040.0122 |journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]] |language=en |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=225–244 |doi=10.1287/moor.1040.0122 |issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> analyzes the effect of network topology on the ''uniqueness'' of the PNE costs:

* A graph ''G'' guarantees that the PNE costs are unique iff ''G'' is a connection [[in series]] of one or more networks of several simple kinds.
* A graph ''G'' does ''not'' guarantee that PNE costs are unique iff ''G'' contains an embedded network of a particular simple type.

Holzman and Law-Yone<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Holzman |first1=Ron |last2=Law-Yone |first2=Nissan |date=1997-10-01 |title=Strong Equilibrium in Congestion Games |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825697905923 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=85–101 |doi=10.1006/game.1997.0592 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> also characterize the networks that guarantee that every atomic CG has a [[Strong Nash equilibrium|strong PNE]], a unique PNE, or a [[Pareto-efficient]] PNE.

Richman and Shimkin<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Richman |first1=Oran |last2=Shimkin |first2=Nahum |date=2007-02-01 |title=Topological Uniqueness of the Nash Equilibrium for Selfish Routing with Atomic Users |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/moor.1060.0229 |journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]] |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=215–232 |doi=10.1287/moor.1060.0229 |issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> characterize the networks that guarantee that every ''splittable'' CG has a unique PNE.

=== General weighted CGs ===
We say that a class ''C'' of functions ''guarantees'' a certain property if every weighted CG in which all delay functions are elements of ''C'' has that property.

* Fotakis, Kontogiannis and Spirakis<ref name=":12" /> prove that the class of [[linear functions]] guarantees the existence of an exact potential, and hence the existence of PNE.
* Panagopoulou and Spirakis<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Panagopoulou |first1=Panagiota N. |last2=Spirakis |first2=Paul G. |date=2007-02-09 |title=Algorithms for pure Nash equilibria in weighted congestion games |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1187436.1216584 |journal=ACM Journal of Experimental Algorithmics |volume=11 |pages=2.7–es |doi=10.1145/1187436.1216584 |s2cid=17903962 |issn=1084-6654|url-access=subscription }}</ref> prove that the class of [[exponential functions]] guarantees the existence of a weighted potential, and hence the existence of PNE.
* Harks, Klimm and Mohring<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Harks |first1=Tobias |last2=Klimm |first2=Max |last3=Möhring |first3=Rolf H. |date=2011-07-01 |title=Characterizing the Existence of Potential Functions in Weighted Congestion Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00224-011-9315-x |journal=Theory of Computing Systems |language=en |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=46–70 |doi=10.1007/s00224-011-9315-x |s2cid=912932 |issn=1433-0490|url-access=subscription }}</ref> prove that a class of functions guarantees the existence of an exact potential, [[if and only if]] it contains only [[affine function]]s. This characterization remain valid when restricted to two-player games, three-resource games, singleton games, games with symmetric strategies, or games with integral weights. Moreover, a class of functions guarantees the existence of a weighted potential, if and only if either (1) it contains only affine functions, or (2) it contains only [[exponential functions]] of the form <math>a_e \cdot \exp{(\phi\cdot x_e)} + b_e</math>, where <math>\phi</math> is the same for all resources. This characterization remain valid when restricted to four-player games, four-resource games, singleton games, games with symmetric strategies, or games with integral weights. For two-player games, a class of functions guarantees the existence of a weighted potential, if and only if all functions in it are of the form <math>a_e \cdot f(x_e) + b_e</math>, where {{mvar|f}} is a monotone function (the same for all resources).
* Harks and Klimm<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Harks |first1=Tobias |last2=Klimm |first2=Max |date=2012-08-01 |title=On the Existence of Pure Nash Equilibria in Weighted Congestion Games |url=https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/moor.1120.0543 |journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]] |language=en |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=419–436 |doi=10.1287/moor.1120.0543 |issn=0364-765X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> prove a similar result for the existence of PNE: they prove that a class of functions guarantees the existence of PNE if and only if either (1) it contains only affine functions, or (2) it contains only [[exponential functions]] of the form <math>a_e \cdot \exp{(\phi\cdot x_e)} + b_e</math>, where <math>\phi</math> is the same for all resources. This characterization remain valid when restricted to three-player games. For two-player games, a class of functions guarantees the existence of PNE if and only if all functions in it are of the form <math>a_e \cdot f(x_e) + b_e</math>, where {{mvar|f}} is a monotone function (the same for all resources).
Gairing, Monien and Tiemann<ref name=":20" /> study weighted network CGs with player-specific delays. They consider both splittable and unsplittable flows. When the delay functions are linear (without a [[constant term]], that is ''b<sub>e</sub>''=0), they introduce two new potential functions and derive results on computation of PNE.

=== Other results ===
There are many other papers about weighted congestion games.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kollias |first1=Konstantinos |last2=Roughgarden |first2=Tim |chapter=Restoring Pure Equilibria to Weighted Congestion Games |date=2011 |editor-last=Aceto |editor-first=Luca |editor2-last=Henzinger |editor2-first=Monika |editor3-last=Sgall |editor3-first=Jiří |title=Automata, Languages and Programming |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-22012-8_43 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=6756 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=539–551 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-22012-8_43 |isbn=978-3-642-22012-8}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ackermann |first1=Heiner |last2=Röglin |first2=Heiko |last3=Vöcking |first3=Berthold |date=2009-04-06 |title=Pure Nash equilibria in player-specific and weighted congestion games |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |series=Internet and Network Economics |language=en |volume=410 |issue=17 |pages=1552–1563 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2008.12.035 |issn=0304-3975|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":13"/>

== Player-specific cost functions ==
The basic CG model can be extended by allowing the delay function of each resource to depend on the player. So for each resource ''e'' and player ''i'', there is a delay function <math>d_{i,e}</math>. Given a strategy <math>P_i</math>, player {{mvar|i}} experiences delay <math>\textstyle \sum_{e \in P_i} d_{i,e}(x_e)</math>.

===<span class="anchor" id="crowding game"></span>Player-specific costs in singleton CGs (crowding games)===
Milchtaich<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=1996-03-01 |title=Congestion Games with Player-Specific Payoff Functions |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825696900275 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=111–124 |doi=10.1006/game.1996.0027 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> introduced and studied '''CGs with player-specific costs''' in the following special case:

* Each player chooses a single resource (such games are called '''singleton CG'''s);
* All players have the same set of strategies.
This special case of CG is also called a '''crowding game'''.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=1998-12-01 |title=Crowding games are sequentially solvable |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s001820050086 |journal=International Journal of Game Theory |language=en |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=501–509 |doi=10.1007/s001820050086 |s2cid=125221 |issn=1432-1270|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2000 |title=Generic Uniqueness of Equilibrium in Large Crowding Games |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3690472 |journal=[[Mathematics of Operations Research]] |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=349–364 |doi=10.1287/moor.25.3.349.12220 |jstor=3690472 |issn=0364-765X}}</ref> It represents a setting in which several people simultaneously choose a place to go to (e.g. a room, a settlement, a restaurant), and their payoff is determined both by the place and by the number of other players choosing the same place.

In a crowding game, given a strategy <math>P_i=\{e\}</math>, player {{mvar|i}} experiences delay <math>d_{i,e}(x_{e})</math>. If the player switches to a different strategy {{mvar|f}}, his delay would be <math>d_{i,f}(x_f+1)</math>; hence, a strategy vector is a PNE iff for every player i, <math>d_{i,e}(x_{e})\leq d_{i,f}(x_{f}+1)</math> for all ''e'',''f''.

In general, CGs with player-specific delays might ''not'' admit a [[Potential game|potential]] function. For example, suppose there are three resources x,y,z and two players A and B with the following delay functions:

* <math>d_{A,x}(1) < d_{A,y}(0) < d_{A,y}(2) < d_{A,z}(0) < d_{A,z}(2) < d_{A,x}(2) </math>
* <math>d_{B,y}(1) < d_{B,x}(0) < d_{B,x}(2) < d_{B,z}(0) < d_{B,z}(2) < d_{B,y}(2) </math>

The following is a cyclic improvement path: <math>(z,y) \to (y,y) \to (y,z) \to (x,z)\to (x,x)\to (z,x) \to (z,y) </math>. This shows that the finite-improvement property does not hold, so the game cannot have a potential function (not even a generalized-ordinal-potential function). However:

* With only two resources, the finite improvement property holds.<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|location=Thm.1}} Hence, a PNE exists.
* With only two players, every finite best-response property holds. Hence, a PNE exists.

When there are three or more players, even best-response paths might be cyclic. However, every CG still has a PNE.<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|location=Thm.2}} The proof is constructive and shows an algorithm that finds a Nash equilibrium in at most <math>{n+1\choose 2} </math> steps. Moreover, every CG is [[Weakly acyclic game|weakly acyclic]]: for any initial strategy-vector, at least one best-response path starting at this vector has a length of at most <math>r{n+1\choose 2} </math>, which terminates at an equilibrium.<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|location=Thm.3}}

Every crowding game is ''sequentially solvable''.<ref name=":14" /> This means that, for every ordering of the players, the [[sequential game]] in which each player in turn picks a strategy has a [[subgame perfect equilibrium|subgame-perfect equilibrium]] in which the players' actions are a PNE in the original simultaneous game. Every crowding game has at least one [[Strong Nash equilibrium|strong PNE]];<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Konishi |first1=Hideo |last2=Le Breton |first2=Michel |last3=Weber |first3=Shlomo |date=1997-01-01 |title=Equilibria in a Model with Partial Rivalry |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022053196922036 |journal=Journal of Economic Theory |language=en |volume=72 |issue=1 |pages=225–237 |doi=10.1006/jeth.1996.2203 |issn=0022-0531|url-access=subscription }}</ref> every strong PNE of a crowding game can be attained as a subgame-perfect equilibrium of a sequential version of the game.<ref name=":14" />

In general, a crowding game might have many different PNE. For example, suppose there are ''n'' players and ''n'' resources, and the negative effect of congestion on the payoff is much higher than the positive value of the resources. Then there are n! different PNEs: every one-to-one matching of players to resources is a PNE, as no player would move to a resource occupied by another player. However, if a crowding game is replicated ''m'' times, then the set of PNEs converges to a single point as ''m'' goes to infinity. Moreover, in a "large" (nonatomic) crowding game, there is generically a unique PNE. This PNE has an interesting graph-theoretic property. Let ''G'' be a [[bipartite graph]] with players on one side and resources on the other side, where each player is adjacent to all the resources that his copies choose in the unique PNE. Then G contains no cycles.<ref name=":15" />

=== Separable cost functions ===
A special case of the player-specific delay functions is that the delay functions can be separated into a player-specific factor and a general factor. There are two sub-cases:

* '''Multiplicatively-separable''' '''cost functions''': <math>d_{i,e}(x_{e}) = a_{i,e}\cdot d(x_e)</math>, where <math>a_{i,e}</math> is a constant that represents the base cost of resource ''e'' to player ''i'', and ''d'' is a general delay function (the same for all resources).
* '''Additively-separable''' '''cost functions''':<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Konishi |first1=Hideo |last2=Le Breton |first2=Michel |last3=Weber |first3=Shlomo |date=1997-10-01 |title=Pure Strategy Nash Equilibrium in a Group Formation Game with Positive Externalities |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S089982569790542X |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=161–182 |doi=10.1006/game.1997.0542 |issn=0899-8256|url-access=subscription }}</ref> <math>d_{i,e}(x_{e}) = a_{i,e} + d(x_e)</math>, where <math>a_{i,e}</math> is a constant that represents the [[fixed cost]] of resource ''e'' to player ''i,'' and ''d'' is a general delay function (the same for all resources).
When only pure-strategies are considered, these two notions are equivalent, since the [[logarithm]] of a product is a sum. Moreover, when players may have resource-specific weights, the setting with resource-specific delay functions can be reduced to the setting with a universal delay function. Games with separable cost functions occur in load-balancing,<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last1=Even-Dar |first1=Eyal |last2=Kesselman |first2=Alex |last3=Mansour |first3=Yishay |chapter=Convergence Time to Nash Equilibria |date=2003 |editor-last=Baeten |editor-first=Jos C. M. |editor2-last=Lenstra |editor2-first=Jan Karel |editor3-last=Parrow |editor3-first=Joachim |editor4-last=Woeginger |editor4-first=Gerhard J. |title=Automata, Languages and Programming |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-45061-0_41 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=2719 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=502–513 |doi=10.1007/3-540-45061-0_41 |isbn=978-3-540-45061-0}}</ref> [[M/M/1 queue]]ing,<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Libman |first1=Lavy |last2=Orda |first2=Ariel |date=2001-08-01 |title=Atomic Resource Sharing in Noncooperative Networks |url=https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016770831869 |journal=Telecommunication Systems |language=en |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=385–409 |doi=10.1023/A:1016770831869 |issn=1572-9451|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[Habitat-selection hypothesis|habitat selection]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Joel S. |date=1990 |title=Habitat Selection as an Evolutionary Game |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2409448 |journal=Evolution |volume=44 |issue=3 |pages=732–746 |doi=10.2307/2409448 |jstor=2409448 |pmid=28567976 |issn=0014-3820|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The following is known about weighted singleton CGs with separable costs:<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Milchtaich |first=Igal |date=2009-11-01 |title=Weighted congestion games with separable preferences |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0899825609000426 |journal=Games and Economic Behavior |language=en |volume=67 |issue=2 |pages=750–757 |doi=10.1016/j.geb.2009.03.009 |issn=0899-8256|hdl=10419/96071 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

* If the base costs <math>a_{i,e}</math> are player-independent (<math>a_{i,e} = a_e</math> for every player ''i''), then the CG has the FIP, hence it has a PNE. The same holds if the base costs are resource-independent (<math>a_{i,e} = a_i</math> for every resource ''e'').<ref name=":3" /><ref name="doi.org">{{Cite book |last1=Fabrikant |first1=Alex |last2=Papadimitriou |first2=Christos |last3=Talwar |first3=Kunal |title=Proceedings of the thirty-sixth annual ACM symposium on Theory of computing |chapter=The complexity of pure Nash equilibria |date=2004-06-13 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1145/1007352.1007445 |series=STOC '04 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=604–612 |doi=10.1145/1007352.1007445 |isbn=978-1-58113-852-8|s2cid=1037326 }}</ref> The proof is based on a vector-valued potential function. For each state of the game, the potential is a vector of size ''n'' containing the costs of all players, sorted from large to small. Whenever a player deviates to a resource with a smaller cost for him, the vector of costs becomes smaller in the [[leximin order]]. 
*If the weights are player-independent (equivalently: the CG is unweighted and the delay-functions are resource-specific), then it has the FIP, hence it has a PNE.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":5" /> If the cost-functions are additively-separable, then the game even has an exact potential function. The result holds even if the cost functions are not monotonically increasing with the load. If the cost-functions are not additively-separable, then FIP may not hold, and there may be no potential function, but a PNE still exists.<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|location=Thm.2}} 
*If the weights are resource-independent, then a PNE exists in the following cases:
**When there are at most ''three'' players, a PNE exists,<ref name=":8">{{Cite book |last1=Mavronicolas |first1=Marios |last2=Milchtaich |first2=Igal |last3=Monien |first3=Burkhard |last4=Tiemann |first4=Karsten |chapter=Congestion Games with Player-Specific Constants |date=2007 |editor-last=Kučera |editor-first=Luděk |editor2-last=Kučera |editor2-first=Antonín |title=Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science 2007 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-74456-6_56 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=4708 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=633–644 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-74456-6_56 |isbn=978-3-540-74456-6}}</ref>{{Rp|location=Cor.3}} though the best-response improvement property might not hold. In contrast, there is a CG with separable costs and resource-independent weights with ''eight'' players in which no PNE exists.<ref name=":6" />{{Rp|location=Thm.3}} 
**When cost functions are additively-separable with linear variable-cost functions, the CG has a weighted potential, hence it has the FIP, hence it has a PNE.<ref name=":8" />{{Rp|location=Thm.6}} 
**When cost functions are additively-separable with logarithmic variable-cost function, and there are at most three players, the CG has the best-response improvement property, hence it has a PNE. However, it might not have the finite-improvement property.<ref name=":20">{{Cite book |last1=Gairing |first1=Martin |last2=Monien |first2=Burkhard |last3=Tiemann |first3=Karsten |chapter=Routing (Un-) Splittable Flow in Games with Player-Specific Linear Latency Functions |date=2006 |editor-last=Bugliesi |editor-first=Michele |editor2-last=Preneel |editor2-first=Bart |editor3-last=Sassone |editor3-first=Vladimiro |editor4-last=Wegener |editor4-first=Ingo |title=Automata, Languages and Programming |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11786986_44 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=4051 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=501–512 |doi=10.1007/11786986_44 |isbn=978-3-540-35905-0}}</ref> For more than three players, the existence of PNE is open.
Every weighted ''singleton'' CG with separable player-specific preferences is isomorphic to a weighted ''network'' CG with player-independent preference.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":9" />

=== Network CGs with player-specific costs ===
Milchtaich considered the special case of CGs with player-specific costs, in which each strategy is a path in a given graph ("network CG"). He proved that every finite game can be represented as an (unweighted) [[network congestion]] game with player-specific costs, with nondecreasing (but not necessarily negative) cost-functions.<ref name=":10" /> A complete characterization of networks that guarantee the existence of PNE in such CGs is posed as an open problem.<ref name=":11" />

== Computing a pure Nash equilibrium ==
=== Computing an equilibrium in unweighted CGs ===
The proof of existence of PNE is constructive: it shows a finite algorithm (an improvement path) that always finds a PNE. This raises the question of how many steps are required to find this PNE? Fabrikant, [[Christos Papadimitriou|Papadimitriou]] and Talwar<ref name="doi.org"/> proved:

* If all strategies are paths in a network ("network CG"), and all players have the same set of strategies ("symmetric CG"), then a PNE can be computed in polynomial time by maximizing the potential, through reduction to [[Minimum-cost flow problem|min-cost flow]]. The algorithm can be adapted to nonatomic CGs: under certain smoothness assumptions, a Nash equilibrium in such a game can be approximated in [[strongly-polynomial time]].
* If the strategies can be general subsets, or the players may have different sets of strategies ("asymmetric CG"), then computing a PNE is [[PLS (complexity)|PLS-complete]]. This implies that there are examples with exponentially-long improvement paths. It also implies that finding a Nash equilibrium reachable from a specified state is [[PSPACE-complete]].
* For every problem in the [[complexity class]] [[PLS (complexity)|PLS]] (essentially, every local search problem), there exists an ordinal potential game with polynomially many players, such that the set of pure Nash equilibria equals the set of local optima.
Even-Dar, Kesselman and Mansour<ref name=":3" /> analyze the number of steps required for convergence to equilibrium in a load-balancing setting.

Caragiannis, Fanelli, Gravin and Skopalik<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |last2=Fanelli |first2=Angelo |last3=Gravin |first3=Nick |last4=Skopalik |first4=Alexander |title=2011 IEEE 52nd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science |chapter=Efficient Computation of Approximate Pure Nash Equilibria in Congestion Games |date=2011-10-01 |pages=532–541 |doi=10.1109/FOCS.2011.50|arxiv=1104.2690 |isbn=978-0-7695-4571-4 |s2cid=14879292 }}</ref> present an algorithm that computes a constant-factor approximation PNE. In particular:

* With linear delay functions, the [[Approximation algorithm|approximation ratio]] is 2+ε, and the runtime is polynomial in the number of players, the number of resources, and 1/ε.
* When delay functions are degree-''d'' polynomials, the approximation ratio is ''d''<sup>O(''d'')</sup>''.''

Their algorithm identifies a short sequence of best-response moves, that leads to an approximate equilibrium. They also show that, for more general CGs, attaining any polynomial approximation of PNE is PLS-complete.

=== Computing an equilibrium in weighted network CGs ===
Fotakis, Kontogiannis and Spirakis<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Fotakis |first1=Dimitris |last2=Kontogiannis |first2=Spyros |last3=Spirakis |first3=Paul |date=2005-12-08 |title=Selfish unsplittable flows |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397505005347 |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |series=Automata, Languages and Programming: Algorithms and Complexity (ICALP-A 2004) |language=en |volume=348 |issue=2 |pages=226–239 |doi=10.1016/j.tcs.2005.09.024 |issn=0304-3975}}</ref> present an algorithm that, in any weighted network CG with linear delay functions, finds a PNE in [[pseudo-polynomial time]] (polynomial in the number of players ''n'' and the sum of players' weights ''W''). Their algorithm is a [[greedy algorithm|greedy]] [[Best response|best-response]] algorithm: players enter the game in descending order of their weight, and choose a best-response to existing players' strategies.

Panagopoulou and Spirakis<ref name=":13" /> show empirical evidence that the algorithm of Fotakis, Kontogiannis and Spirakis in fact runs in time polynomial in ''n'' and log ''W''. They also propose an initial strategy-vector that dramatically speeds this algorithm.

In general, a weighted network CG may not have a PNE. Milchtaich<ref name=":11" /> proves that deciding whether a given weighted network CG has a PNE is NP-hard even in the following cases:

* There are two players; all players are allowed to use all paths; all cost-functions are nonnegative.
* There are two players; the CG is unweighted; the costs are player-specific and nonnegative.

The proof is by reduction from the directed edge-disjoint paths problem.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fortune |first1=Steven |last2=Hopcroft |first2=John |last3=Wyllie |first3=James |date=1980-02-01 |title=The directed subgraph homeomorphism problem |journal=Theoretical Computer Science |language=en |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=111–121 |doi=10.1016/0304-3975(80)90009-2 |issn=0304-3975|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Caragiannis, Fanelli, Gravin and Skopalik<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Caragiannis |first1=Ioannis |last2=Fanelli |first2=Angelo |last3=Gravin |first3=Nick |last4=Skopalik |first4=Alexander |date=2015-03-27 |title=Approximate Pure Nash Equilibria in Weighted Congestion Games: Existence, Efficient Computation, and Structure |url=https://doi.org/10.1145/2614687 |journal=ACM Transactions on Economics and Computation |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=2:1–2:32 |doi=10.1145/2614687 |s2cid=5581666 |issn=2167-8375|url-access=subscription }}</ref> present an algorithm that computes a constant-factor approximation PNE in weighted CGs. In particular:

*With linear delay functions, the approximation ratio is <math>\frac{3+\sqrt{5}}{2}+O(\epsilon)</math>, and the runtime is polynomial in the number of players, the number of resources, and 1/ε.
* When delay functions are degree-''d'' polynomials, the approximation ratio is <math>d^{2d + o(d)}</math>''.''

To prove their results, they show that, although weighted CGs may not have a potential function, every weighted CG can be ''approximated'' by a certain potential game. This lets them show that every weighted CG has a (''d''!)-approximate PNE. Their algorithm identifies a short sequence of best-response moves, that leads to such an approximate PNE.

== Summary of congestion game classifications ==
In summary, CGs can be classified according to various parameters:

* Number and splittability of players: '''atomic''' '''CG''', '''splittable CG''' or '''nonatomic CG''';
* Weight of players: '''unweighted''' '''CG''' or '''weighted''' '''CG''' (with '''resource-independent weights''' or '''resource-specific weights''');
* Cost functions for different players using the same resource: '''identical''' or '''player-specific''' (with '''separable''' or '''nonseparable''' cost-functions).
* Possible strategies: one resource ('''singleton''' '''CG''') or path in a network ('''network CG''') or any subset ('''general CG)'''.
* Strategy sets of different players: different ('''asymmetric CG''') or identical ('''symmetric CG''').

V. |year=1990 |title=Resource allocation games |journal=Computational Mathematics and Modeling |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=433 |doi=10.1007/BF01128293|s2cid=120639586 }}</ref><ref name=":4" /> are somewhat related to congestion games.
* '''Incomplete information''': Facchini, van Megen, Borm and Tijs<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Facchini |first1=Giovanni |last2=van Megen |first2=Freek |last3=Borm |first3=Peter |last4=Tijs |first4=Stef |date=1997-03-01 |title=Congestion Models and Weighted Bayesian Potential Games |url=https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1004991825894 |journal=Theory and Decision |language=en |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=193–206 |doi=10.1023/A:1004991825894 |s2cid=123623707 |issn=1573-7187|url-access=subscription }}</ref> extend Rosenthal's model to a setting with [[incomplete information]]. They prove that the related [[Bayesian game]]s are potential games, and therefore have pure [[Bayesian Nash equilibrium|Bayesian-Nash equilibria]].
* '''Coalitions''': Fotakis, Kontogiannis and Spirakis<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Fotakis |first1=Dimitris |last2=Kontogiannis |first2=Spyros |last3=Spirakis |first3=Paul |chapter=Atomic Congestion Games Among Coalitions |date=2006 |editor-last=Bugliesi |editor-first=Michele |editor2-last=Preneel |editor2-first=Bart |editor3-last=Sassone |editor3-first=Vladimiro |editor4-last=Wegener |editor4-first=Ingo |title=Automata, Languages and Programming |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/11786986_50 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=4051 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=572–583 |doi=10.1007/11786986_50 |isbn=978-3-540-35905-0}}</ref> study CGs in which players participate in coalitions.
* '''Congestion games in nature:''' Milinsky<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Milinski |first=Manfred |date=2010-04-26 |title=An Evolutionarily Stable Feeding Strategy in Sticklebacks |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1439-0310.1979.tb00669.x |journal=Zeitschrift für Tierpsychologie |language=en |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=36–40 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0310.1979.tb00669.x|url-access=subscription }}</ref> describes an experiment in which a natural CG converges into a Nash equilibrium. In his experiment, he fed six [[stickleback]]s from two ends of a tank. The fish distribution between the two ends was, on average, similar to the ratio of the food supply rates, so that no individual fish could increase his feeding rate by moving to the other side. Milchtaich<ref name=":0" /> presents a more general treatment of CGs in [[interspecific competition]].
